title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
takeaway: Visible status, familiar language, recovery, and user control help people understand outcomes and choose their next step.
decision: Show the active feed mode and confirm explicit feedback; keep reset and recovery actions easy to find.

title: Display Applied Filters in an Overview
takeaway: Applied-filter summaries give immediate confirmation and make it easier to broaden results without reopening hidden filter panels. These observations come from ecommerce and are adapted to content discovery.
decision: Keep selected topics and languages visible near the feed and provide direct removal or reset controls.

title: Hick’s Law
takeaway: More numerous or complicated choices can slow decisions; progressive disclosure can reduce initial cognitive load.
decision: Keep a small primary set of feed controls and place detailed preference tuning behind a clearly labeled control.

title: Priority Guides: A Content-First Alternative to Wireframes
takeaway: Prioritize real content by user goals before arranging the layout, starting with the most important mobile information.
decision: Put the real product display, concrete product value, and account action ahead of decorative marketing; prioritize useful content rather than time spent.

title: Infinite Scrolling, Pagination Or Load More Buttons? Usability Findings In eCommerce
takeaway: The authors distinguish exploratory browsing from ranked search and identify footer access and return-position problems with automatic infinite loading. This is not direct evidence about a news feed.
decision: For ranked topic results, prefer an explicit batch/end state and preserve the reader’s position; treat a manual Load more option as a recommended refinement rather than optimizing endless scrolling.

title: Context is the new interface
takeaway: Preferences and past behavior should inform continuity without becoming unquestioned assumptions; people need to inspect and correct the context used.
decision: Explain which explicit interests influence the feed and allow clearing learned preferences without changing the person’s account.

title: Learned Helplessness in AI-Assisted Work: When Users Stop Trying to Shape the Tools They Use
takeaway: Corrections need visible consequences and acknowledgements so users can see a connection between their input and system behavior.
decision: When Show less is selected, confirm the change and actually reduce the relevant signal; do not display success if persistence fails.

title: Talk to Me! Feedback and Notifications in Mobile Design
takeaway: Feedback should fit the person’s goal, arrive promptly, and avoid unnecessary interruption or arbitrary gamification.
decision: Use one concise status update after a save, share, or relevance adjustment; avoid repeated engagement prompts, artificial streaks, and unrelated badges.

title: Search — Material Design
takeaway: Search helps people locate content in a large information space; predictable access and suitable search patterns improve discovery. This is stable legacy guidance, not a claim about a new 2026 trend.
decision: Keep topic search discoverable, retain the active query, and distinguish search results from a general personalized feed.

title: Accessibility — Atlassian Design
takeaway: Consistency, plain language, personal control, text alternatives, and respecting motion preferences are part of end-to-end accessible experiences.
decision: Label personalization actions in plain language, include text with state icons, and preserve account and OS motion preferences.

title: Focus management — Primer
takeaway: Keyboard focus must remain visible, follow a logical order, enter new dialogs, and return to a sensible place after they close.
decision: Relevance menus and reset dialogs should be keyboard-operable and return focus to their trigger; card drag actions must retain a standard button alternative.

title: Content — Carbon Design System
takeaway: Clear, purposeful interface language and standardized terminology make navigation and product behavior more coherent.
decision: Use one label per outcome across the app: Saved, Shared, Show less, Latest, and For you; avoid interchangeable terms that imply different ranking behavior.

title: App Design Guidelines — Shopify
takeaway: Matching the appearance and behaviors of the surrounding product reduces relearning and supports trust across workflows.
decision: Make feed controls and recommendation feedback use the same buttons, spacing, and input behavior as communities and settings.

title: Writing for errors — Adobe Spectrum
takeaway: Useful error messages explain what happened and provide a concrete path forward; the component should fit the consequence of the failure.
decision: Keep failed feed loads and failed preference saves contextual, preserve the reader’s current state, and provide Try again instead of silently resetting the feed.

title: Design principles — Fluent 2
takeaway: Familiar platform behavior, less visual clutter, and inclusion help people stay focused on their own task.
decision: Give article/video content more visual weight than recommendation controls, while keeping those controls discoverable and consistent on mobile.

title: Notification banner — GOV.UK Design System
takeaway: A notification banner is for relevant service-wide or cross-page information; not every contextual message belongs in a prominent banner.
decision: Confirm per-card feedback near the card or in a concise status region; reserve a service banner for a feed-wide outage or important cross-page change.

title: Checklist — The A11Y Project
takeaway: Plain content, keyboard access, semantics, labels, media alternatives, and contrast need to be checked together; a checklist alone does not guarantee accessibility.
decision: Review new feed controls with keyboard-only navigation and visible focus, and keep every icon action named and usable without hover.

title: Design for understanding — Digital.gov
takeaway: Logical structure, descriptive headings, scanning aids, and restrained emphasis make content easier to understand.
decision: Use descriptive feed headings and readable article metadata; make the current mode understandable without a paragraph of algorithm jargon.

title: Accessibility — Designsystemet
takeaway: Accessible base components still rely on correct semantic HTML, focus management, language metadata, token use, and meaningful content.
decision: Use native controls and the app’s semantic tokens for feed preferences; treat language selection as meaningful content filtering and preserve accessible labels.

title: Design Systems Gallery — Design Systems Repo
takeaway: The curated product gallery exposes established design systems whose patterns connect reusable components with real product implementations. It is a reference directory, not an independent outcome study.
decision: Use documented product patterns and real app components as references; show the actual implemented interface in the landing preview rather than an invented mock product.

title: Design Systems Report 2026
takeaway: The practitioner survey distinguishes component adoption measures from outcome measures and reports continuing gaps in accessibility, patterns, and documentation.
decision: Evaluate the feed by successful discovery, saves, correction usefulness, and low error rates; do not treat longer sessions or more scrolling alone as proof of value.

title: Building Accessibility Into a Canvas-Based Product
takeaway: Figma’s engineering account shows that a visually rich interaction must also expose synchronized focus, semantics, and announcements for keyboard and screen-reader users.
decision: Keep personalization and card actions represented in semantic DOM controls with announced outcomes, even where the visible interaction also supports dragging or motion.
